          Diego Gómez, Brighton and the Rise in Premier League Shots from the Halfway Line
        
      
                          
                      Oct 23, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Ithiel Piñero / Data Viz, Jonathan Manuel / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
After Diego Gómez’s goal against Crystal Palace, Brighton are closing in on the Premier League record for shots from 50 metres or more in a season. So, we ask: why?

It’s impossible to know whether the increased adoption of expected goals is the sole reason, part of the reason, or plays no part whatsoever, but it's intriguing that the metric’s popularity has coincided almost perfectly with shots being taken closer to goal.

Perhaps this would have happened regardless of the advancement of football analytics. As coaching improved and became more detailed, teams may well have trained to get the ball closer to goal simply because what xG tells us is already obvious: the closer to goal you shoot from, the more likely you are to score.

Whatever the reason, though, the data proves Premier League football has been based less around shooting from long distance in recent years. The first six seasons for which this data is available (from 2003-04) are the six highest for the proportion of shots taken from outside the penalty area. They are the only seasons on record that have seen more than 45% of shots attempted from range.

And the five most recent, from 2022-23 to 2026-27, have produced the lowest numbers of all seasons on record, each seeing 35% or fewer shots attempted from outside the penalty area. That fits with what we’d expect, given the aforementioned focus on getting the ball closer to goal.

Whether they have been the main driving force behind the change, data-savvy clubs have played a big role. Thomas Frank spoke about “making the chance bigger” while in charge of Brentford, and for three seasons running, his side were among the Premier League’s top two teams for the average xG value of each shot they attempted.

In other words, Brentford, a club known for and who have had huge success with their data-led approach, consistently waited patiently for opportunities to create high-quality chances rather than shooting from long range.

Doing so is the sign of a good team. Teams who can work the ball closer to goal to “make the chance bigger” are going to be able to score goals more reliably. Shooting from distance is a high-risk strategy that has become increasingly unpopular over the years because it is less likely to bring reward.

However, Brighton, another of the Premier League’s most noteworthy and successful proponents of a heavily data-led approach in both their recruitment and their tactics, appear to be bucking the trend.

Diego Gómez’s remarkable strike in the 5-0 win over Crystal Palace on Sunday was struck from 51.3 metres out, putting it eighth on the list of Premier League goals scored from furthest out over the period for which this data is available (from 2006-07).
Eight of the other nine goals were scored nine seasons or more ago. And when it comes to the players to take the most shots from more than 50m, Charlie Adam is miles clear at the top.

The fact he is so far clear, with 25 attempts, and the kind of names alongside him on this list shows how much more common shooting from this distance was in a different time. It’s not something teams have tended to do in recent years.
In the days of Adam, these were largely pot shots that were perhaps a little ill-advised; his Blackpool side attempted a record nine in 2010-11 without hitting the target even once, for example.

But could it be the case that there is some consideration to Gómez’s attempts? It’s certainly curious he is doing it for a team as data focused as Brighton. Little that the club does happens by chance, after all.

Interestingly, most of the shots from distance this season have been by Brighton players. Of the 14 attempted from 50 metres or more in the Premier League in 2026-27, six have been by Brighton players. That’s 42.9%. They account for 6.5% of all shots from anywhere on the pitch.
Their total of six shots from 50m+ just seven games into 2026-27 is already the second-highest total by a team on record in a Premier League season, behind that Blackpool team mentioned above.
So, is there something else at play here? Have Brighton’s analysts spotted an opportunity from which they are trying to gain an edge. Is there a plan in place to threaten from very long range?
Manager Fabian Hürzeler was asked about the topic after Gómez’s goal on Sunday and was unequivocal in his response. “We don't train shots from 50 metres,” he said.

This kind of attempt must have some degree of opportunism around it, and some of Brighton’s long-range shots are particularly optimistic attempts to take advantage of an out-of-position goalkeeper. One example is Chema Andrés’ attempt against Arsenal when David Raya was way out of his goal after sweeping up.
But the numbers we’ve just looked at suggest there may be some instruction – or at the very least, an allowance – for Brighton players to try scoring from far out in normal play.
